drills.los_text: demonstrate how an asset's returns may be replicated by using options

questions.stem: Under put-call parity, the two equivalent portfolios are most likely:

options.A: A call and a bond, versus a put and the underlying.
options.B: The underlying and a call, versus a put and a bond.
options.C: A call and the underlying, versus a put and a bond.

rationales.A: Put-call parity shows the equivalence (or parity) of a portfolio of a call and a risk-free bond with a portfolio of a put and the underlying, which leads to the relationship between put and call prices: S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T. The fiduciary call, c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T, and the protective put, S₀ + p₀, have identical payoffs at expiration — a floor at the strike X with participation above it — so arbitrage forces their current costs to be equal. Rearranged, the relationship gives c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − X/(1 + r)^T and p₀ = c₀ − S₀ + X/(1 + r)^T.
rationales.B: This pairs the underlying with the call and the risk-free bond with the put, giving S₀ + c₀ = p₀ + X/(1 + r)^T. The parity relationship runs the other way: the underlying pairs with the put and the risk-free bond pairs with the call, so the correct statement is S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T. Holding the underlying together with a call is a leveraged bullish position, not one side of the parity identity.
rationales.C: This reverses the pairing by grouping the call with the underlying. Parity equates the fiduciary call — the call plus the risk-free bond, c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T — with the protective put — the put plus the underlying, S₀ + p₀. The call is grouped with the bond because the bond supplies the strike at expiration, and the put is grouped with the underlying because the put supplies the floor.

questions.stem: Under put-call-forward parity, the two equivalent portfolios are most likely:

options.A: A call and the discounted forward price, versus a put and a bond.
options.B: A put and the discounted forward price, versus a call and a bond.
options.C: A put and the underlying spot, versus a call and a bond.

rationales.A: This places the present value of the forward price with the call rather than with the put, which misstates which portfolios are equivalent. The forward belongs with the put, because a long forward plus the present value of the forward price replicates the underlying and so turns the put into a synthetic protective put: F₀(T)/(1 + r)^T + p₀ = c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T.
rationales.B: Put-call-forward parity identifies the equivalence between buying a fiduciary call, given by the purchase of a call and the risk-free bond, and a synthetic protective put. The latter involves the purchase of a put option and a forward contract on the underlying that expires at the same time as the put option: F₀(T)/(1 + r)^T + p₀ = c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T. The substitution works because a long forward plus a bond paying F₀(T) at expiration delivers the underlying at T, so its present value F₀(T)/(1 + r)^T stands in for S₀ in ordinary put-call parity.
rationales.C: This is ordinary put-call parity, which uses the spot price of the underlying: S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + X/(1 + r)^T. Put-call-forward parity substitutes the present value of the forward price, F₀(T)/(1 + r)^T, for the spot price, which is what allows the relationship to be expressed with a forward contract in place of a position in the underlying.

questions.stem: A long call combined with a short put at the same strike price and expiration, on the same underlying, is most likely equivalent to:

options.A: A long forward position.
options.B: A long put position.
options.C: A long straddle position.

rationales.A: The combination of a long call and a short put with identical strike price and expiration, traded at the same time on the same underlying, is equivalent to a synthetic long forward position. The long call creates the upside and the short put creates the downside on the underlying. Whatever the price of the underlying at expiration, one of the two options is in the money, so the investor effectively buys the underlying at the strike price: the payoff is S_T − X, identical to a forward struck at X. By put-call parity the net premium paid, c₀ − p₀, equals S₀ − X/(1 + r)^T, the present value of that forward's built-in gain or loss.
rationales.B: A long call combined with a short put is a synthetic long forward, not a synthetic long put. A synthetic long put is built from a short position in the underlying (or a short forward or futures position) combined with a long call. The position described here gains as the underlying rises and loses as it falls, the opposite of a long put's exposure.
rationales.C: A long straddle is a long call plus a long put at the same strike and expiration — two long options, a volatility position that profits from a large move in either direction and loses the combined premium if the underlying finishes near the strike. Here the put is sold rather than bought, which removes the downside protection and leaves a directional long exposure equivalent to a forward.

questions.stem: A synthetic short forward position is most likely created by:

options.A: Buying a call and a put at the same strike and maturity.
options.B: Buying a call and selling a put at the same strike and maturity.
options.C: Selling a call and buying a put at the same strike and maturity.

rationales.A: Buying both a call and a put at one strike and maturity is a long straddle, a volatility position that profits from a large move in either direction and has no net directional exposure near the strike. A synthetic short forward must lose value as the underlying rises, which a long call prevents.
rationales.B: Buying a call and selling a put at the same strike and maturity is a synthetic long forward: the long call creates the upside and the short put creates the downside, so the payoff rises with the underlying and mirrors the underlying itself. That is the exact opposite of the synthetic short forward being asked about.
rationales.C: A trader can create a synthetic short forward position by selling a call and buying a put at the same strike price and maturity. The short call gives away the gains above the strike and the long put produces the gains below it, so the payoff is X − S_T: the exact opposite of the synthetic long forward position, which is long the call and short the put.

questions.stem: A synthetic long put is most likely created by:

options.A: Combining long stock with a short call.
options.B: Combining short stock with a long call.
options.C: Combining long stock with a long call.

rationales.A: Long stock combined with a short call is a covered call. Its payoff is capped above the strike and fully exposed below it, which resembles a short put rather than a long put: the position loses as the underlying falls, whereas a long put gains.
rationales.B: A short stock position, or a short forward or futures position, combined with a long call creates the synthetic long put. The symmetric payoff of the short stock position becomes asymmetrical once the investor buys the call: the call caps the loss if the stock rises, while the short stock keeps the gain if the stock falls. The payoffs from this synthetic put position at various stock prices at option expiration are identical to those of a long put at the same strike — with a 50-strike call, gains accrue below 50 and losses above 50 are limited to the call premium net of any proceeds on the short stock.
rationales.C: Long stock combined with a long call doubles the bullish exposure instead of creating a put; the position gains as the underlying rises, the opposite of a long put. The synthetic long put pairs a short position in the underlying (or a short forward) with a long call.

questions.stem: The motivation for creating a synthetic long forward position is most likely to:

options.A: eliminate the underlying's downside risk.
options.B: avoid the margin required on an actual forward.
options.C: exploit arbitrage against the actual forward price.

rationales.A: A synthetic long forward — a long call plus a short put at the same strike and expiration — retains the full downside of the underlying. As the underlying falls below the strike, the short put obligates purchase at the strike, so losses accumulate exactly as they would on the underlying itself. Keeping the upside while eliminating the downside describes a protective put, which costs a premium, not a synthetic forward, which is entered at little or no net cost. The motivations for the synthetic position are to exploit an arbitrage opportunity presented by the actual forward price, or to obtain an alternative to the outright purchase of a long forward.
rationales.B: Margin treatment is incidental rather than a motivation. The two motivations are arbitrage against the actual forward price and the need for an alternative route to long forward exposure. Where customization matters, a forward contract is frequently used instead of futures to acquire a stock position precisely because the contract terms can be tailored — but that is a reason to prefer a forward over a future, not a reason to synthesize the forward out of options.
rationales.C: The motivation to create a synthetic long forward position could be to exploit an arbitrage opportunity presented by the actual forward price, or the need for an alternative to the outright purchase of a long forward position. The synthetic is built from a long call and a short put struck at the forward price with the same expiration, which reproduces the forward's payoff line one for one; if the actual forward is mispriced relative to that combination, the two can be traded against each other for an arbitrage profit. Frequently a forward contract is used instead of futures to acquire a stock position because it allows for contract customization.

questions.stem: A market maker hedges a short forward position by buying a call and writing a put, both struck at the forward price with the same expiration. If the underlying is above the strike at expiry, she most likely:

options.A: bears an unhedged loss on the rally.
options.B: exercises the call and delivers the shares.
options.C: buys the shares in the open market.

rationales.A: The synthetic long forward neutralizes the rally scenario rather than leaving it open. With the underlying above the strike, she exercises the long call, pays the strike times the number of shares, receives the shares, delivers them to the client, and receives the forward price times the number of shares. Because the strike equals the forward price, those two cash flows offset exactly, so a rally produces neither gain nor loss on the hedged position.
rationales.B: At the expiry of the forward contract, if the share price is above the strike, the market maker exercises her call, pays the strike times the number of shares, receives the shares, then delivers those shares to the client and receives the forward price times the number of shares. If the price is below the strike, the mirror image holds: the owner of the long put exercises, the market maker receives the shares for the strike, then delivers them to the client and again receives the forward price. Since the strike was set equal to the forward price, the position is fully hedged in both directions, and the market maker's compensation is the bid-offer spread rather than any directional gain.
rationales.C: Waiting until expiration and buying shares at the prevailing market price leaves the price risk unhedged for the whole life of the forward: if the underlying rises, the market maker pays more for the shares than the forward price she will receive on delivery. The synthetic long forward — long call plus short put struck at the forward price — locks the purchase price in at inception, which is the entire point of the hedge.

drills.los_text: discuss the investment objective(s), structure, payoff, risk(s), value at expiration, profit, maximum profit, maximum loss, and breakeven underlying price at expiration of a covered call position

questions.stem: A covered call position is most likely composed of:

options.A: long stock and a long put.
options.B: long stock and a long call.
options.C: long stock and a short call.

rationales.A: Long stock plus a long put is a protective put: the investor pays a premium to insure the shares against a decline below the strike. A covered call is the opposite trade in the options leg — the call is written, so the premium is received, the downside is cushioned only by that premium, and the upside is capped rather than protected.
rationales.B: Long stock plus a long call is not a covered call; paying a further premium for a long call merely amplifies the bullish exposure instead of monetizing it. Nor is it a straddle, which is a long call plus a long put. A covered call requires writing the call against shares already held, so that the premium is received and the shares stand ready for delivery if the call is exercised.
rationales.C: A covered call is long stock plus a short call. A long position in 100 shares of the underlying is required for each short call contract, and no additional cash margin is needed if that long position in the underlying is maintained, because the shares themselves secure the obligation. If the stock price exceeds the strike price at expiry, the underlying shares are called away from the covered call writer and delivered to satisfy the option holder's right to buy shares at the strike price.

questions.stem: The most common motivation for writing covered calls is most likely:

options.A: protection against a large decline in the underlying.
options.B: cash generation in anticipation of limited upside.
options.C: profit from a sharp rise in the underlying's volatility.

rationales.A: This confuses the covered call with a protective put. A short call cushions a decline only by the amount of the premium received, so the breakeven falls to the stock price less the premium; below that point the writer absorbs the full decline in the shares, down to a maximum loss of the stock price less the premium. The structure generates income, it does not provide meaningful downside protection.
rationales.B: The most common motivation for writing covered calls is cash generation in anticipation of limited upside moves in the underlying. The call option writer keeps the premium regardless of what happens in the future, and some investors view that premium as an additional source of income similar to cash dividends. Essentially, writing the call expresses the view that the volatility of the underlying asset will be lower than the pricing of the option suggests.
rationales.C: Writing a call is a short-volatility position. The premium received is the most the option leg can ever earn, so the writer profits when realized volatility turns out to be lower than the implied volatility embedded in the option's price. Expecting volatility to rise sharply is an argument for buying options, not for writing them against a share position.

questions.stem: For a covered call, the maximum gain, maximum loss, and breakeven price are most likely:

options.A: strike plus premium, stock price plus premium, and strike less premium.
options.B: premium only, unlimited, and strike plus premium.
options.C: appreciation to the strike plus premium, stock price less premium, and stock price less premium.

rationales.A: The signs are wrong. Maximum gain is the appreciation to the exercise price plus the premium, (X − S₀) + c₀, not X + c₀, which would credit the writer with the entire strike rather than the rise in the shares up to it. Maximum loss is S₀ − c₀, not S₀ + c₀: the premium received offsets part of the loss instead of adding to it. Breakeven is measured from the price paid for the shares, S₀ − c₀, not from the exercise price.
rationales.B: Maximum loss on a covered call is not unlimited. The writer owns the shares that would be delivered, so the worst case is the stock falling to zero, a loss of S₀ − c₀. Unlimited loss describes a naked short call, where the writer must buy shares at any price to meet delivery. Maximum gain is also understated: it is (X − S₀) + c₀, the appreciation to the exercise price plus the premium, not the premium alone, and breakeven is S₀ − c₀ rather than X + c₀.
rationales.C: Maximum gain = (X − S₀) + c₀; maximum loss = S₀ − c₀; breakeven price = S₀ − c₀. The maximum gain is the appreciation to the exercise price plus the option premium, because any appreciation past the exercise price is lost to the call buyer. The maximum loss would occur if the stock became worthless: the investor loses the stock price but keeps the premium, so the loss equals the original stock price less the premium. The breakeven occurs when the stock falls by exactly the premium received, which is why the breakeven and the maximum loss are the same value for a covered call.

questions.stem: At expiration, the value of a covered call is most likely:

options.A: the stock price less the call's exercise value.
options.B: the stock price less the put's exercise value.
options.C: the stock price plus the call's exercise value.

rationales.A: Covered call expiration value = S_T − Max[(S_T − X), 0]. At option expiration the value is the stock price minus the exercise value of the call, because any appreciation beyond the exercise price belongs to the option buyer and is therefore a liability of the writer. The profit at option expiration is that value plus the option premium received minus the original price of the stock: S_T − Max[(S_T − X), 0] + c₀ − S₀.
rationales.B: This substitutes the put payoff, Max[(X − S_T), 0], for the call payoff that was actually written against the shares. The option sold in a covered call is a call, so the claim against the position arises when S_T exceeds X, not when it falls below X. Using the put payoff would reduce the position's value in a falling market, where in fact the writer simply holds depreciating shares, and would leave the upside uncapped, where in fact it stops at X.
rationales.C: Adding the call's exercise value treats the investor as long the call. The covered call writer is short the call, so Max[(S_T − X), 0] is an obligation and the term is subtracted: S_T − Max[(S_T − X), 0]. Adding it would imply the position gains twice over above the exercise price, when the defining feature of the structure is that the payoff is capped at X.

questions.stem: For a covered call, the relationship between the breakeven price and the maximum loss is most likely:

options.A: the breakeven lies above the maximum loss by the premium.
options.B: the breakeven lies above the maximum loss by the strike less the stock price.
options.C: the breakeven and the maximum loss are the same.

rationales.A: This separates two figures that coincide. Breakeven is S₀ − c₀ and the maximum loss is also S₀ − c₀, so the gap between them is zero rather than c₀. The premium does enter both expressions, but it enters each the same way: it lowers the price at which the position recovers its cost, and it lowers the worst-case loss, by the identical amount.
rationales.B: Breakeven is measured from the initial stock price, S₀ − c₀, not from the exercise price. Using X − c₀ overstates the breakeven by X − S₀ whenever the call is written out of the money, and it would place the breakeven above the maximum loss by that difference. In fact the two values coincide at S₀ − c₀.
rationales.C: With a covered call, the breakeven price and the maximum loss are the same value, both equal to S₀ − c₀. The breakeven represents the price at which the position exactly recovers the cost of the stock net of the premium received. The maximum loss is the initial net cost of the position — the stock price less the premium received — and it is realized when the stock goes to zero. Because the net outlay is S₀ − c₀ in both cases, the two figures are identical.

questions.stem: An investor buys a stock at 25.00 and writes a call on it with an exercise price of 30.00 for a premium of 1.55. At expiration the stock trades at 31.33. The maximum gain on the covered call is closest to:

rationales.A: The covered call writer participates in gains up to the exercise price, after which further appreciation is lost to the call buyer. That is, X − S₀ = 30.00 − 25.00 = 5.00. The call writer also keeps c₀, the option premium, which is 1.55. So the total maximum gain is (X − S₀) + c₀ = 5.00 + 1.55 = 6.55, and it is reached at any terminal price at or above the 30.00 exercise price, including the 31.33 observed here.
rationales.B: This computes (S_T − S₀) − c₀ = 31.33 − 25.00 − 1.55 = 4.78, which nets the premium in the wrong direction and ignores the call away at 30.00. The writer receives the premium, so it is added rather than subtracted, and the share appreciation that accrues to the writer stops at the exercise price instead of running all the way to the terminal price.
rationales.C: This computes (S_T − X) + c₀ = 31.33 − 30.00 + 1.55 = 2.88, taking the terminal price as the starting point for the writer's share gain. The covered call's upside stops at the exercise price, so the appreciation term is X − S₀ = 5.00, giving a maximum gain of (X − S₀) + c₀ = 6.55.

questions.stem: An investor buys a stock at 25.00 and writes a call on it with an exercise price of 30.00 for a premium of 1.55. At expiration the stock trades at 31.33. The breakeven stock price is closest to:

rationales.A: The call premium of 1.55 offsets a decline in the stock price by the amount of the premium received: breakeven = S₀ − c₀ = 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45. Below that price the position loses money, and the loss grows one for one with the shares until the stock reaches zero, where the loss equals the full 23.45.
rationales.B: This computes X + c₀ = 30.00 + 1.55 = 31.55, which is not the breakeven of any part of this position. Breakeven is measured from the price paid for the shares rather than from the exercise price, and the premium is subtracted because it cushions a fall in the stock instead of raising the level the stock must reach. The correct breakeven is S₀ − c₀ = 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45.
rationales.C: This computes S_T − c₀ = 31.33 − 1.55 = 29.78, substituting the terminal price for the purchase price. The breakeven is a property of the position as entered and depends only on S₀ and c₀; the terminal price is the outcome being compared against the breakeven, so it cannot be an input to it. The correct breakeven is 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45.

questions.stem: An investor buys a stock at 25.00 and writes a call on it with an exercise price of 30.00 for a premium of 1.55. At expiration the stock trades at 31.33. The maximum loss on the covered call is closest to:

rationales.A: 2.88 is S_T − X + c₀ = 31.33 − 30.00 + 1.55, a figure built from the upside of the position rather than its downside, so it cannot be the maximum loss. The maximum loss arises in the opposite scenario: the stock falling to zero, which costs the investor the price paid for the shares less the premium kept, S₀ − c₀ = 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45.
rationales.B: This uses the terminal price in place of the price paid: S_T − c₀ = 31.33 − 1.55 = 29.78. The investor's capital at risk is what was paid for the shares net of the premium received, not what the shares happen to be worth at expiration, so the maximum loss is S₀ − c₀ = 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45.
rationales.C: The stock price can fall to zero, causing a loss of the entire investment, but the option writer still keeps the option premium received: maximum loss = S₀ − c₀ = 25.00 − 1.55 = 23.45. This is also the breakeven price of the covered call, since for this structure the breakeven and the maximum loss are the same value.

questions.stem: Porto holds 5,000 shares of PBR at 15.84 per share and writes PBR September 15 calls for a premium of 1.64. If the calls are exercised, her effective sale price per share is closest to:

rationales.A: 15.84 is the stock's original market price, which is what Porto would have received by simply selling the shares outright. It ignores the 1.64 premium she already collected for writing the call, and that premium is the entire source of the price improvement the strategy produces.
rationales.B: 15.00 is the strike price alone: the amount received when the call is exercised and the shares are delivered. It omits the 1.64 premium received at the time the call was written, so it understates the effective proceeds by exactly that premium.
rationales.C: Porto receives 1.64 when she writes the call and 15 when the call is exercised, so she has effectively sold the stock at 15 + 1.64 = 16.64. She could simply have sold the shares at their original price of 15.84; in this situation the option strategy instead produced a price improvement of (15 + 1.64) − 15.84 = 0.80 per share, or about 5.05%, over roughly a month. Writing calls against a position she is willing to sell converts the option's time value into incremental sale proceeds, at the cost of giving up any appreciation above the strike.

questions.stem: An American call option's premium is most likely:

options.A: Time value subtracted from exercise value.
options.B: Time value plus the put's exercise value.
options.C: Time value plus the call's exercise value.

rationales.A: The premium is the sum of exercise (intrinsic) value and time value, not the difference. Subtracting time value would push the premium of an at-the-money or in-the-money option below its exercise value, and no option trades below the value obtainable by exercising it. Call Premium = Time Value + Max(0, S − X).
rationales.B: Max(0, X − S) is the exercise value of a put, not a call. A call has exercise value only when the underlying trades above the strike, so the correct intrinsic term is Max(0, S − X). The time value component here is right; the intrinsic component belongs to the wrong option type.
rationales.C: An American option premium can be viewed as having two parts, exercise value (also called intrinsic value) and time value: Call Premium = Time Value + Intrinsic Value = Time Value + Max(0, S − X). Someone who writes covered calls to improve on the market is capturing the time value, which augments the stock selling price. The offset is that giving up part of the return distribution results in an opportunity loss if the underlying rises above the strike.

questions.stem: A protective put is most likely analogous to:

options.A: Selling insurance.
options.B: Buying insurance.
options.C: Using leverage.

rationales.A: The protective-put holder buys insurance: he pays the premium rather than collecting it. The party selling insurance for premium income is the option writer, such as a covered-call writer, whose position and motivation are the opposite of the protective-put buyer's.
rationales.B: The protective put is often viewed as a classic example of buying insurance. The investor holds a risky asset, wants protection against a loss in value, and buys that protection in the form of the put. The exercise price of the put is similar to the coverage amount of an insurance policy, and the difference between the current asset price and the strike price is similar to the policy deductible. A protective put with a low exercise price is therefore like an insurance policy with a high deductible: less expensive, but the holder absorbs more of the price decline before the payoff begins.
rationales.C: A put floors the downside rather than amplifying it. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses, whereas a protective put reduces risk: the loss is capped at the depreciation to the exercise price plus the premium paid, while the upside on the stock is retained.

questions.stem: For a protective put, the maximum gain, maximum loss, and breakeven at expiration are most likely:

options.A: Gain capped at the strike, loss limited to the premium, breakeven above the strike.
options.B: Unlimited gain, loss limited to the decline to the strike plus the premium, breakeven above the initial price.
options.C: Gain capped at the strike plus the premium, unlimited loss, breakeven at the strike.

rationales.A: The gain on a protective put is not capped. The investor still owns the stock, which can rise to any level, so the upside is unlimited. The loss is also larger than the premium alone, because the stock can fall all the way to the exercise price before the put's floor engages; the premium is lost on top of that decline.
rationales.B: The stock can rise to any level and the position benefits fully from the appreciation, so the maximum gain is unlimited (theoretically). On the downside, losses are cut off once the stock price falls to the exercise price, so the maximum loss is the depreciation to the exercise price plus the premium paid: S₀ − X + p₀. Breakeven = initial stock price + option premium = S₀ + p₀, because the premium must be recovered before the position profits. At expiration the position is worth the greater of the stock price or the exercise price.
rationales.C: The loss direction is reversed. The long put caps the downside, so the loss is limited rather than unlimited, and it is the gain that is open-ended because the investor continues to hold the stock. Breakeven also sits above the initial stock price, not at the strike, since the premium must first be earned back.

questions.stem: At expiration, the value of a protective put is most likely:

options.A: The stock price plus the put's payoff.
options.B: The stock price minus the put's payoff.
options.C: The stock price plus a call's payoff.

rationales.A: The value of the protective put at expiration is the greater of the stock price or the exercise price, because the stock can rise to any level but has a floor value equal to the put's exercise price: Value of Protective Put at Expiration = S_T + Max[(X − S_T), 0]. Profit is the ending value minus the beginning value: Profit = S_T + Max[(X − S_T), 0] − S₀ − p₀, that is, the terminal stock value plus the put payoff, less the cost of the stock and the premium paid for the put.
rationales.B: Subtracting the put payoff treats the investor as short the put. The protective-put holder is long the put, so its payoff is added to the terminal stock value; subtracting it would deepen the loss as the stock fell instead of flooring the position.
rationales.C: Max(S_T − X, 0) is a call payoff, which rewards a rise in the underlying. The protective put's floor comes from the put payoff, Max(X − S_T, 0), which pays off only when the stock finishes below the exercise price — precisely the outcome the insurance is bought against.

questions.stem: To reduce the cost of put protection on a stock holding, a portfolio manager is most likely to:

options.A: Buy a put with a lower exercise price.
options.B: Buy a put with a higher exercise price.
options.C: Buy a put with a longer maturity.

rationales.A: The portfolio manager can reduce the cost of the insurance by increasing the size of the deductible, that is, the current stock price minus the put exercise price, which means choosing a put with a lower exercise price. Moving the strike down from 15 to 14 on a stock trading near 15.84 lowers the premium, but the put then provides no protection against losses in the stock until it has fallen to 14.00 per share. The cheaper insurance is paid for by absorbing more of the decline.
rationales.B: A higher exercise price shrinks the deductible and raises the premium, because the put starts paying off sooner and covers more of the potential decline. That buys more protection at greater cost, which is the opposite of the cost-reduction move.
rationales.C: Longer-dated puts carry higher premiums, not lower, because they hold more time value. The lever for cutting the cost of the insurance is strike selection: a lower exercise price enlarges the deductible and cheapens the put.

questions.stem: The relationship between a put's value and its time until expiration is most likely:

options.A: Nonlinear.
options.B: Linear, with a constant daily decay in time value.
options.C: Linear, so doubling the maturity doubles the price.

rationales.A: There is not a linear relationship between the put value and its time until expiration. A two-month option does not sell for twice the price of a one-month option, nor does a three-month option sell for three times the price of a one-month option. Time value grows at a decreasing rate, so each additional month of protection costs less than the month before it. The practical consequence is that rolling short-dated puts repeatedly is dearer per year of cover than buying a single longer-dated put.
rationales.B: Time decay is not constant. It accelerates as expiration approaches, so the daily erosion of value on a 30-day put is larger than on a 90-day put, and the loss is fastest in the option's final days.
rationales.C: This assumes value scales in proportion to time. It does not: a two-month put sells for less than twice a one-month put, because option time value grows at a decreasing rate with maturity rather than proportionally.

questions.stem: Theta on a long protective put position is most likely:

options.A: Negative and larger for the longer-dated put.
options.B: Positive, so the put gains value each day.
options.C: Negative, so the put loses value each day.

rationales.A: This reverses the relationship. The shorter-dated option has the larger, more negative theta: a 30-day put with a theta of −0.015 loses more value per day than a 90-day put with a theta of −0.009. Buying the cheaper short-dated put therefore means accepting faster daily erosion of the premium paid.
rationales.B: A long option holder loses to the passage of time, so theta on a long put is negative, representing daily erosion of value. Positive theta belongs to the writer of the option, who benefits as time value decays.
rationales.C: Theta values on long option positions are negative, approximating the daily loss in value as time passes. A November 15 put with 90 days to expiration has a theta of −0.009, while a September 15 put with 30 days has a theta of −0.015, so buying the cheaper short-dated put brings greater daily erosion of value than the more expensive longer-dated one. The decay is also uneven across the option's life: if the stock remains at 15.84, the Black-Scholes-Merton value of the put erodes to zero over the last 10 days to maturity at varying rates averaging about −0.03 per day.

questions.stem: Once the feared adverse event has occurred, the holder of a protective put is most likely to:

options.A: Sell the put.
options.B: Hold the put to expiration.
options.C: Hold the put until implied volatility falls.

rationales.A: A price shock to the underlying asset might increase the market's expectations of future volatility, thereby likely increasing the put premium, and by selling the option early the investor would capture this increase. Equally important, once the adverse event has occurred there may be no reason to continue to hold the insurance. If the investor no longer needs it, he should cancel it and get part of the purchase price back: he should sell the put and recapture some of its cost.
rationales.B: Holding to expiration surrenders exactly what has become valuable. The remaining time value, inflated by the higher volatility expectations the shock produced, is realised only by selling; carried to expiry it decays to zero, and the protection is no longer needed once the feared event has already happened.
rationales.C: A price shock typically raises, rather than depresses, the market's expectation of future volatility, which inflates the put's resale value. Waiting for volatility to subside gives that inflated component back; capturing it is precisely the argument for selling the put early.

questions.stem: Continuously purchasing protective puts over the long term is most likely:

options.A: Cheaper per year of protection than one long-dated put.
options.B: Advisable for any equity portfolio.
options.C: Expensive enough to erase most of the long-term gain.

rationales.A: Option time value does not scale linearly with maturity: a one-month put costs more than half a two-month put, so repeatedly rolling short-dated puts is an especially expensive route to continuous cover, not a cheap one. Either way, paying premiums year after year remains a material drag on long-term returns.
rationales.B: Continuous protection is not advisable as a standing policy for an equity portfolio. The repeated premium outlays can consume the equity risk premium the portfolio exists to earn, which is why the strategy is reserved for temporary, identified exposures rather than carried permanently.
rationales.C: Such continuous purchasing of puts to protect against a possible stock price decline is an expensive strategy that would wipe out most of the long-term gain on an otherwise good investment. The occasional purchase of a protective put to manage a temporary situation, however, can be a sensible risk-reducing activity: insurance bought against a specific exposure for a limited period is affordable, whereas insurance carried continuously is not.

drills.los_text: compare the delta of covered call and protective put positions with the position of being long an asset and short a forward on the underlying asset

questions.stem: The position delta of a covered call consisting of 100 long shares and one short at-the-money call option is closest to:

rationales.A: The delta of the 100-share position is 100 × +1 = +100. Because the call is at the money, meaning the stock price and the exercise price are equal, it has a delta of approximately 0.5. The portfolio is short one call contract, and from the portfolio's perspective the delta of that short call is −0.5 × 100 = −50, because a short call loses money as the underlying rises. The covered call therefore has a position delta of +100 − 50 = +50.
rationales.B: +100 is the delta of the 100-share stock leg on its own and ignores the written call. The short at-the-money call contributes −0.5 × 100 = −50, so the hedged position cannot retain the full +100 directional exposure.
rationales.C: A position delta of zero would require the short call to offset the stock entirely, which would need a call delta near 1.0, as on a deep-in-the-money call. An at-the-money call has a delta of roughly 0.5, so writing it removes only half the stock exposure, leaving +50.

questions.stem: The position delta of a protective put consisting of 100 long shares and one long at-the-money put option is closest to:

rationales.A: +100 ignores the put leg entirely. The at-the-money put has a delta of approximately −0.5, so the contract contributes −0.5 × 100 = −50 and offsets half of the stock's +100 delta, leaving a position delta of +50 rather than +100.
rationales.B: The long 100 shares contribute a delta of 100 × +1 = +100. The long at-the-money put has a delta of approximately −0.5, so one contract contributes −0.5 × 100 = −50. The protective put's position delta is +100 − 50 = +50, the same position delta as an at-the-money covered call built from long 100 shares and one short at-the-money call: +100 points for the stock and −50 points for the option leg.
rationales.C: Zero would require a deep-in-the-money put with a delta near −1.0, which would fully offset the stock. An at-the-money put with a delta near −0.5 only halves the exposure, leaving a position delta of +50.

questions.stem: The position delta of a long position in 100 shares combined with a short forward position on 50 shares of the same non-dividend-paying stock is closest to:

rationales.A: +100 is the delta of the long 100-share leg on its own. The short forward on 50 shares contributes −50, so the full +100 exposure does not survive the hedge.
rationales.B: The short forward covers only 50 of the 100 long shares, so it cancels half the exposure rather than all of it. A position delta of zero would require a short forward on the full 100 shares.
rationales.C: Futures and forwards on non-dividend-paying stocks are essentially proxies for the stock, so their deltas are 1.0 for a long position and −1.0 for a short position. The long 100 shares contribute +100 and the short forward on 50 shares contributes −50, so the short forward cancels half the long stock position and the position delta is +100 − 50 = +50.

questions.stem: An at-the-money covered call, an at-the-money protective put, and a long stock/short forward position that each carry a position delta of +50 are most likely:

options.A: equivalent for moves of any size.
options.B: identical in maximum loss.
options.C: similar only for small moves.

rationales.A: Equal position delta buys only local, small-move equivalence. The three positions differ in gamma, vega, theta and in the shape of their full payoff profiles, so they are not equivalent for a move of any size.
rationales.B: Equal deltas imply similar behavior only for small moves, and maximum losses differ. The protective put's downside is cut off at the put's strike, whereas the covered call and the long stock/short forward combination remain exposed to a much larger decline.
rationales.C: These three positions — an at-the-money covered call, an at-the-money protective put, and a long stock/short forward position — all have the same position delta of +50, so for small movements in the price of the underlying asset they show very similar gains and losses. The equivalence is local only: past small moves the positions diverge, because their gamma, vega, theta and full payoff profiles are different.

drills.los_text: compare the effect of buying a call on a short underlying position with the effect of selling a put on a short underlying position

questions.stem: An investor who is short a stock and buys a call option on it most likely:

options.A: offsets losses when the share price rises.
options.B: offsets losses when the share price falls.
options.C: stays exposed to unlimited losses in a rally.

rationales.A: To offset the risks of a short position, an investor may purchase a call, making the new portfolio (call − stock). The long call offsets portfolio losses when the share price increases: above the strike, the call payoff rises point for point with the further loss on the short stock. Losses are therefore bounded rather than open-ended, never exceeding the strike less the short entry price plus the premium paid — 1.13 in the worked case.
rationales.B: A short stock position loses money when the price rises, not when it falls; a decline is where the short position earns its profit. The long call hedges the upside, so it is not what offsets losses on a price decrease.
rationales.C: The long call caps the loss on the short position. Above the strike, gains on the call match any further loss on the short stock, so the combined loss is bounded at roughly the strike minus the short entry price plus the premium paid, not unlimited.

questions.stem: An investor who is short a stock and writes a put option on it most likely:

options.A: reduces gains as the stock falls.
options.B: obtains full protection against a rally.
options.C: gains without limit as the stock falls.

rationales.A: To generate income from option premiums, an investor who is short the stock may also sell a put, making the portfolio (− put − stock). As the stock drops in value the investor profits on the short stock position, but those portfolio gains are reduced by the losses on the written put below its strike. When the share price increases, the short position loses money while the put expires worthless, so the investor keeps the put premium; the loss on the short position can still be substantial but is somewhat reduced by that premium.
rationales.B: The put premium is only a small cushion against a rally. Once the share price rises above the short entry price by more than the premium received, losses on the short stock keep accumulating, so the protection is far from complete.
rationales.C: The short put caps the downside gain. Below the put's strike, losses on the written put offset any further profit on the short stock, so portfolio gains stop growing instead of increasing without limit.

questions.stem: The delta of short PBR shares is −1, the delta of the SEP 16 PBR call is 0.516, and the delta of the SEP 15 PBR put is −0.335. The portfolio deltas of short stock plus a long SEP 16 call and of short stock plus a short SEP 15 put are most likely:

options.A: identical to each other.
options.B: positive with the long call.
options.C: negative with both options.

rationales.A: The two deltas are not the same: 0.516 − 1 = −0.484 for the long call structure against −1 − (−0.335) = −0.665 for the short put structure. A long call and a short put both contribute positive delta here, but of different magnitude — 0.516 versus 0.335 — so the structures do not coincide.
rationales.B: The combined delta of the short shares and the long call is 0.516 − 1 = −0.484, which is negative. Buying the call makes the position less bearish than the short stock alone, but it does not make it bullish.
rationales.C: The delta from the short PBR shares is −1. Adding the SEP 16 call, with a delta of 0.516, gives an overall portfolio delta of 0.516 − 1 = −0.484, still negative and so still a bearish strategy, only less bearish than the short alone. Writing the SEP 15 put instead contributes −(−0.335) = +0.335, giving a position delta of −1 + 0.335 = −0.665, which is also negative and only slightly less bearish because of the put premium. Both structures therefore stay bearish.

questions.stem: For an investor who is short a stock, the vega and theta obtained from buying a call rather than from writing a put are most likely:

options.A: identical for the two structures.
options.B: absent in both structures.
options.C: long vega and negative theta with the call.

rationales.A: The signs flip between the structures. Buying the call makes the investor long vega with negative theta, while writing the put makes the investor short vega with positive theta, so the exposures are opposite rather than the same.
rationales.B: Both option legs carry real vega and theta. The call buyer pays time decay of −0.018 per day in exchange for positive volatility exposure of 0.018, and the put writer is short vega of −0.017 while earning theta of +0.015 per day. The stock leg has neither vega nor theta, but it does not cancel the option's.
rationales.C: Buying the call against the short stock position makes the investor long vega, 0.018, and leaves the position exposed to time decay, because theta is −0.018 per day. Writing a put against the short position instead makes the investor short vega, −0.017, and a beneficiary of time decay, since theta on the short put is +0.015 (= −[−0.015]).

questions.stem: The payoff profile of writing a put and that of writing a covered call are most likely:

options.A: opposite, because the strategies are unrelated.
options.B: similar, because both are long volatility.
options.C: similar, because of put-call parity.

rationales.A: Put-call parity gives P = C − S + PV of X, implying −P ≈ −C + S once the present value of the exercise price is ignored. A short put's payoff therefore resembles a covered call rather than opposing it, and the two strategies are closely related.
rationales.B: Writing a put and writing a covered call are both short-volatility positions, because each sells an option rather than buying one. Their resemblance follows from put-call parity, not from a long-vega view.
rationales.C: The two strategies are very similar because of put-call parity. P = C − S + PV of X implies that −P ≈ −C + S, ignoring PV of X, which shows that a short put payoff profile is similar to that of a covered call.

drills.los_text: discuss the investment objective(s), structure, payoffs, risk(s), value at expiration, profit, maximum profit, maximum loss, and breakeven underlying price at expiration of the following option strategies: bull spread, bear spread, straddle, and collar

questions.stem: The two options in a money spread most likely differ by:

options.A: exercise price.
options.B: expiration date.
options.C: strike price and underlying asset.

rationales.A: In a money spread the two options differ only by exercise price: the investor buys an option with a given expiration and exercise price and sells an option with the same expiration but a different exercise price, both on the same underlying asset. The term spread is used because the payoff is based on the difference, or spread, between the option exercise prices.
rationales.B: Options that differ only in expiration date, holding the exercise price fixed, make up a calendar or time spread. A money spread keeps the expiration the same and differs by exercise price.
rationales.C: A money spread's two options are written on the same underlying asset and differ only by strike. A structure spanning two different underlyings would not be a money spread at all.

questions.stem: Regarding the distinction between debit and credit option spreads, the most accurate statement is that a debit spread:

options.A: produces a net cash inflow at initiation.
options.B: requires a net cash payment at initiation.
options.C: is distinguished from a credit spread by using calls rather than puts.

rationales.A: A net cash inflow at initiation is what defines a credit spread, not a debit spread. In a debit spread the long option is worth more than the written option, so the premium paid exceeds the premium received and the investor funds the position with a net payment.
rationales.B: If establishing the spread requires a cash payment by the investor, it is referred to as a debit spread. Debit spreads are effectively long because the long option value exceeds the short option value. If the spread initially results in a cash inflow to the investor, it is referred to as a credit spread; credit spreads are effectively short because the short option value exceeds the long option value. The net initial cash flow, not the choice of option type, is the test.
rationales.C: Either calls or puts can form a debit spread or a credit spread. A bull spread built with calls is a debit spread because the lower-strike call bought costs more than the higher-strike call written, while the same bull spread built with puts is a credit spread. The classification turns on the direction of the initial cash flow, not on whether the legs are calls or puts.

questions.stem: A bull call spread is most likely constructed by:

options.A: buying the lower-strike call and writing the higher-strike call.
options.B: writing the lower-strike call and buying the higher-strike call.
options.C: buying both the lower-strike call and the higher-strike call.

rationales.A: A bull call spread buys the lower-strike call (more expensive, c_L) and writes the higher-strike call (less expensive, c_H). Regardless of whether a bull spread is constructed with puts or with calls, the strategy requires buying one option and writing another with a higher exercise price. Because the higher exercise price call is less expensive than the lower-strike call, c_L > c_H and the position involves an initial cash outflow: a debit spread with net premium V₀ = c_L − c_H.
rationales.B: Reversing the legs — writing the lower-strike call and buying the higher-strike call — creates a bear call spread. Because the call written is the more expensive one, that position generates an initial cash inflow and is a credit spread, not a bull call debit spread.
rationales.C: Buying both calls leaves no offsetting short leg, so the position is not a spread at all. Without the written higher-strike call there is no premium received to reduce the cost and no cap on the payoff, so neither the cost nor the risk profile of a bull spread is obtained.

questions.stem: The maximum gain on a bull call spread is most likely equal to:

options.A: the net premium paid.
options.B: the difference in exercise prices less the net premium paid.
options.C: the difference in exercise prices plus the net premium paid.

rationales.A: The net premium paid, c_L − c_H, is the maximum loss rather than the maximum gain. That loss is realized when S_T ≤ X_L, because both calls then expire out of the money and the investor forfeits the entire cost of establishing the spread.
rationales.B: Max gain = X_H − X_L − (c_L − c_H), achieved when S_T ≥ X_H. If S_T is below X_L the strategy loses a limited amount: when both options expire out of the money the investor loses the net premium, c_L − c_H. The profit on the upside, if S_T is at least X_H, is likewise limited to the difference in strike prices minus the net premium. The breakeven follows from Π = S_T* − X_L − c_L + c_H = 0, giving S_T* = X_L + c_L − c_H, the lower exercise price plus the cost of the spread.
rationales.C: This adds the net premium instead of subtracting it. The premium paid to establish the spread is a cost, so it reduces rather than augments the strike-width gain; the most that can be earned is X_H − X_L − (c_L − c_H).

questions.stem: An October 45 call trades at 2.55 and an October 50 call at 1.45, with the underlying at 44.50. The maximum gain on a 45/50 bull call spread is closest to:

rationales.A: With a bull spread, the maximum gain occurs at the high exercise price. At an underlying price of 50 or higher, the spread is worth the difference in the strike prices, or 50 − 45 = 5. The cost of establishing the spread is the price paid for the lower-strike option minus the price received for the higher-strike option: 2.55 − 1.45 = 1.10. The maximum gain is therefore 5.00 − 1.10 = 3.90.
rationales.B: 1.10 is the net cost of the spread, 2.55 − 1.45. That outlay is the maximum loss on the position, incurred when the underlying finishes at or below 45 and both calls expire worthless, not the maximum gain.
rationales.C: The maximum gain is the strike width minus the net cost: (50 − 45) − 1.10 = 3.90. A value of 3.05 understates the gain by netting the premiums against the wrong base; the full 5.00 strike width is available at expiration once the underlying reaches 50.

questions.stem: A bear put spread is most likely constructed by:

options.A: buying the higher-strike put and writing the lower-strike put.
options.B: buying the lower-strike put and writing the higher-strike put.
options.C: buying both the higher-strike put and the lower-strike put.

rationales.A: With a bear spread, an investor buys the higher exercise price and writes the lower exercise price. When this strategy is done with puts, the higher exercise price option costs more than the lower exercise price option, so the investor has a debit spread with an initial cash outlay of p_H − p_L, which is the most he can lose.
rationales.B: Buying the cheaper lower-strike put and writing the more expensive higher-strike put produces an initial cash inflow, which is a bull put (credit) spread. A bear put spread does the opposite: it buys the higher strike and writes the lower.
rationales.C: Buying two puts provides no offsetting written leg, so the position is not a bear put spread. Without the short lower-strike put there is no premium received to offset the cost and no floor on the payoff, so the bounded profit and loss profile of the spread is not obtained.

questions.stem: An October 45 put trades at 2.92 and an October 50 put at 6.80. The maximum loss on a 45/50 bear put spread is closest to:

rationales.A: 4.38 does not equal the net debit on the spread. Because a bear put spread buys the higher strike and writes the lower, the maximum loss is the initial outlay: 6.80 − 2.92 = 3.88.
rationales.B: The bear put spread buys the October 50 put and writes the October 45 put, so the initial cash outlay is the cost of the October 50 put minus the premium received from writing the October 45 put: 6.80 − 2.92 = 3.88. Because the position is a debit spread, that initial outlay is the most the investor can lose, and it is lost whenever the underlying finishes at or above 50 and both puts expire worthless.
rationales.C: 1.12 is not the net premium paid. The debit is the cost of the long October 50 put minus the premium received on the short October 45 put: 6.80 − 2.92 = 3.88, and that initial outlay is the maximum loss.

questions.stem: An October 45 call trades at 2.55 and an October 50 call at 1.45. The breakeven underlying price for a 45/50 bull call spread is closest to:

rationales.A: 48.88 does not equal the lower strike plus the net cost of the spread. The breakeven is 45 + 1.10 = 46.10; a price near 48.88 would already be well inside the profitable region of the position.
rationales.B: 47.50 is the midpoint of the two exercise prices, which has no bearing on the breakeven. The breakeven is the lower strike plus the net cost of the spread: 45 + (2.55 − 1.45) = 46.10.
rationales.C: The investor breaks even when the position is worth the price she paid. The long call is worth 1.10 at a stock price of 46.10, and the October 50 call expires out of the money and is thus worthless. The breakeven price is the lower exercise price of 45 plus the 1.10 cost of the spread, or 46.10.

questions.stem: On a given underlying, a long straddle is most likely constructed by:

options.A: buying a call and a put with the same exercise price and expiration.
options.B: buying a call and a put with different exercise prices and the same expiration.
options.C: buying a call and writing a put with the same exercise price and expiration.

rationales.A: A long straddle is an option combination in which one buys both puts and calls, with the same exercise price and same expiration date, on the same underlying asset. It is a directional play on the underlying's volatility, expressing the view that volatility will increase from current levels, so the trade is said to be long volatility. Because the buyer pays premium on two options, a large price movement in either direction is needed before the position turns profitable.
rationales.B: Buying a call and a put at different exercise prices describes a strangle, not a straddle. The straddle uses the same exercise price for both legs, which is what makes its payoff symmetric about that single strike.
rationales.C: A long call combined with a short put at the same exercise price and expiration is a synthetic long forward, a purely directional position with no volatility exposure of the straddle's kind. A long straddle is long both options, so it profits from a large move in either direction.

questions.stem: At initiation, an at-the-money long straddle most likely has:

options.A: a delta near zero and a gamma near zero.
options.B: a delta near one and a low gamma.
options.C: a delta near zero and a high gamma.

rationales.A: The delta of an at-the-money straddle is indeed near zero, because the positive delta of the long call is nearly offset by the negative delta of the long put. Gamma, however, is high rather than near zero: both legs are at the money, where the rate of change of delta is at its greatest, so the position's delta moves quickly as the underlying moves.
rationales.B: This reverses the two Greeks. An at-the-money straddle is close to delta-neutral, with a delta near zero rather than near one, and its gamma is high rather than low.
rationales.C: The long straddle initially has a very low delta (about +0.07 in a representative at-the-money position) together with a high gamma (about 0.14). The trader does not initially favor an increase or a decrease in the share price but knows the delta may change quickly. Once a direction, up or down, asserts itself, the position takes on a non-zero delta value.

questions.stem: The value of a long straddle at expiration is most likely equal to:

options.A: the call's payoff less the put's payoff.
options.B: the call's payoff alone.
options.C: the call's payoff plus the put's payoff.

rationales.A: Subtracting the put's payoff would describe a long call combined with a short put, a synthetic long forward. The long straddle is long both options, so their payoffs are added: V_T = Max(0, S_T − X) + Max(0, X − S_T).
rationales.B: This omits the long put leg entirely. Below the exercise price the call expires worthless and the straddle's value comes wholly from the put, Max(0, X − S_T), which is the source of the position's profit on a large downward move.
rationales.C: The value of a straddle at expiration is the combined value of the call and the put: V_T = Max(0, S_T − X) + Max(0, X − S_T). Profit is V_T less the premiums paid, Π = Max(0, S_T − X) + Max(0, X − S_T) − c₀ − p₀. There are two breakeven points: the lower at S_TL* = X − c₀ − p₀ and the upper at S_TH* = X + c₀ + p₀. Underlying prices in the range between them produce a loss, with the largest loss, the full premium outlay, occurring at S_T = X.

questions.stem: For the buyer of a straddle, it is most likely that:

options.A: maximum loss is unlimited.
options.B: maximum gain is limited to the premium paid.
options.C: maximum gain is unlimited.

rationales.A: A large move in either direction produces a gain for the straddle buyer, not an unlimited loss: the buyer holds both a call and a put, so one leg acquires positive exercise value whichever way the stock goes. The buyer's loss is capped at the total premium paid, c₀ + p₀, and that worst case arises only when the stock closes exactly at the strike, where both options expire worthless. Unlimited exposure to a sharp move belongs to the writer of the straddle, not to the buyer.
rationales.B: This confuses the buyer's limited loss with the gain. It is the maximum loss that is limited to the total premium paid, c₀ + p₀, incurred when the stock closes exactly at the strike and both the put and the call expire worthless. The maximum gain is not bounded by the premium: the long call gives the straddle buyer theoretically unlimited upside, because the stock can rise to any level.
rationales.C: The stock can rise to any level, so profit on the long call leg has no ceiling and the long straddle's maximum gain is theoretically unlimited on the upside. The maximum loss is limited to the total premium paid for the two positions, c₀ + p₀, and occurs when the stock closes exactly at the strike price, because both the put and the call then expire worthless. At any other price one of the two options has a positive exercise value, so the risk of a long straddle is limited to the amount paid for the two option positions.

questions.stem: A collar is most likely composed of:

options.A: no share position, with two calls struck at different prices.
options.B: a long share position, with a long put struck below and a short call struck above.
options.C: a short share position, with a long at-the-money call and a long at-the-money put.

rationales.A: Buying one call and writing another at a different strike, with no position in the underlying, is a call spread. A collar is built around an existing holding: the long underlying position supplies the exposure, the purchased put caps the downside, and the written call finances that protection. With no underlying position there is nothing being collared.
rationales.B: A collar is an option position in which the investor is long shares of the underlying, then buys a put with an exercise price below the current stock price and writes a call with an exercise price above the current stock price. The put delivers downside protection, as in a protective put, while writing the covered call reduces the cash outlay; by selecting the options carefully, an investor can often offset most of the put premium paid with the call premium received. Profit and loss on the equity position is therefore limited on both sides by the option positions.
rationales.C: The collar is built on a long underlying position, protected below by an out-of-the-money put and financed by a written out-of-the-money call. A short underlying position combined with a long at-the-money call and a long at-the-money put is neither protective nor self-financing: buying both options pays out two premiums instead of offsetting one against the other, and the resulting payoff is not the bounded long-equity profile of a collar.

questions.stem: A zero-cost collar is most likely constructed by:

options.A: buying a put and writing a call at the same strike price.
options.B: buying a put and writing a call with the same premium.
options.C: buying a put and buying a call whose premiums offset.

rationales.A: Zero cost comes from matching premiums, not strikes. If the put and the call shared one exercise price, the protective range would collapse to that single price, fixing the payoff rather than leaving a band between a floor and a cap, and there is no reason the two premiums would be equal at a common strike in any case.
rationales.B: A zero-cost collar involves the purchase of a put and the sale of a call with the same premium, so the call premium received offsets the put premium paid and the structure is put on at no net cash outlay. A collar written in the over-the-counter market can be easily structured to provide a precise offset of the put premium with the call premium. Most collars are structured and transacted over the counter for exactly this reason: the exercise price on the call must be a specific one, and listed strikes rarely price out to an exact offset.
rationales.C: A collar writes the call in order to finance the put; it does not buy both. Buying a put and a call together is a straddle, a long volatility position that costs two premiums, so the premiums add rather than offset and the position cannot be structured at zero net cost.

questions.stem: At expiration, the value of a collar on a long underlying position is most likely equal to:

options.A: the underlying's value plus the long put's payoff less the short call's payoff.
options.B: the underlying's value less the long put's payoff plus the short call's payoff.
options.C: the greater of the underlying and the call strike, less the lesser of the underlying and the put strike.

rationales.A: The value of the collar at expiration is the sum of the value of the underlying asset, the value of the long put (struck at X₁), and the value of the short call (struck at X₂): V_T = S_T + Max(0, X₁ − S_T) − Max(0, S_T − X₂), where X₂ > X₁. The profit is the profit on the underlying share plus the profit on the long put and the short call, so that Π = S_T + Max(0, X₁ − S_T) − Max(0, S_T − X₂) − S₀ − p₀ + c₀. Below X₁ the long put offsets further declines in the share, and above X₂ the written call surrenders further gains, which is why the payoff is bounded at both ends.
rationales.B: The signs are reversed. The investor is long the put, so its expiration value Max(0, X₁ − S_T) is added, and short the call, so its expiration value Max(0, S_T − X₂) is subtracted: V_T = S_T + Max(0, X₁ − S_T) − Max(0, S_T − X₂). Subtracting the put's payoff and adding the call's would describe an investor who has sold the floor and bought the cap — the mirror image of a collar, with the downside left open and the upside geared rather than capped.
rationales.C: This max/min construction does not reproduce the collar's payoff: it is worth X₂ − X₁ at every price between the strikes and it rises as the share falls below X₁, which is the opposite of a hedged long position. The collar's expiration value is V_T = S_T + Max(0, X₁ − S_T) − Max(0, S_T − X₂), which equals X₁ at or below the put strike, S_T between the strikes, and X₂ at or above the call strike.

questions.stem: As a collar's put and call exercise prices move successively farther in opposite directions from the current price, the position's risk–return profile is most likely to:

options.A: remain unchanged.
options.B: converge on a risk-free fixed-income return.
options.C: replicate a long position in the underlying.

rationales.A: Strike placement is the entire lever on a collar's profile, so the profile cannot be unaffected by the choice of put and call exercise prices. A collar is economically intermediate between pure equity and fixed-income exposure, and where it sits within that range is set by how far the two strikes are placed from the current price.
rationales.B: The convergence runs the other way. Wider strikes make the collar more equity-like; it is as the chosen strike prices approach and meet each other that expected returns and volatility become less and less equity-like and eventually converge on those of a risk-free fixed-income return to the time horizon.
rationales.C: As the chosen put and call exercise prices move successively farther in opposite directions from the current price, the combined collar position begins to replicate the underlying gain/loss pattern of a long position in the underlying security: the floor sits well below and the cap well above, so most of the share's movement passes through to the holder. Conversely, as the chosen strike prices approach and meet each other, the expected returns and volatility become less and less equity-like and eventually converge on those of a risk-free fixed-income return to the time horizon. A collar position is thus, economically, intermediate between pure equity and fixed-income exposure.

questions.stem: For a bear spread built by buying a put at the higher exercise price and writing a put at the lower exercise price, the breakeven stock price at expiration is most likely:

options.A: the higher exercise price less the net premium paid.
options.B: undefined.
options.C: the lower exercise price plus the long put's premium.

rationales.A: For a bear put spread with lower strike X_L (the short put, premium p_L) and higher strike X_H (the long put, premium p_H), the breakeven is S_T* = X_H − p_H + p_L: the higher strike reduced by the net premium paid, p_H − p_L, which is the point that sets profit equal to zero between the strike prices. Profit between the strikes is X_H − S_T − p_H + p_L. The maximum loss, at or above X_H where both puts expire worthless, is −(p_H − p_L) = p_L − p_H; the maximum gain, at or below X_L, is X_H − X_L − p_H + p_L. With a higher strike of 16, a long put premium of 1.96 and a short put premium of 1.46, breakeven is 16 − 1.96 + 1.46 = 15.50.
rationales.B: The breakeven is well defined: S_T* = X_H − (p_H − p_L), the higher exercise price less the net premium paid. Both legs being puts is no obstacle. The spread is established for a net debit of p_H − p_L, and the stock need only fall far enough below the higher strike for the long put's exercise value to recover that debit, which happens at a single, calculable price.
rationales.C: Breakeven sits at the higher strike less the net premium, X_H − (p_H − p_L), not at the lower strike plus the long put's premium: the premium received on the written put reduces the cost of the position and so raises, rather than lowers from X_L, the price at which profit turns positive. Note also that the spread's maximum gain, X_H − X_L − p_H + p_L, arrives when the stock falls to or below the lower strike, not when it rallies above the higher strike, where both puts expire worthless and the loss is the net premium.

questions.stem: The two legs of a calendar spread most likely differ only in:

options.A: option type.
options.B: expiration date.
options.C: underlying asset.

rationales.A: A call and a put sharing one strike and one expiration is a straddle, not a calendar spread. The legs of a calendar spread are the same type of option, both calls or both puts, written on the same underlying at the same strike; it is the expiration date that differs.
rationales.B: A strategy in which one sells an option and buys the same type of option (put or call) but with different expiration dates, on the same underlying asset and with the same strike, is commonly referred to as a calendar spread. When the investor buys the more distant option and sells the near-term option, it is a long calendar spread; buying a near-term option and selling a longer-dated one is a short calendar spread. Because only the expiration date differs, the position is a trade on time value and implied volatility rather than on direction.
rationales.C: The same underlying asset is required. Two options of the same type and expiration written on different underlyings form a relative-value trade between two assets, with no difference in expiry to exploit; a calendar spread's legs are identical in type, strike and underlying and differ only in when they expire.

questions.stem: The primary motivation for a long calendar spread is most likely to:

options.A: capture the dividend paid on the underlying.
options.B: take advantage of time decay.
options.C: profit from a large directional move.

rationales.A: Dividend capture is not the rationale for the structure. A long calendar spread is long a longer-dated option and short a nearer-dated option of the same type and strike, and its return comes from the faster erosion of time value in the written short-dated option, not from any cash flow paid on the underlying.
rationales.B: A portion of the option premium is time value, and time value decays over time, approaching zero as the option expiration date nears. Taking advantage of this time decay is a primary motivation behind a calendar spread. Time decay is more pronounced for a short-term option than for one with a long time until expiration, so the trade seeks to exploit this characteristic by purchasing a longer-term option and writing a shorter-term option: the written option's time value erodes faster than that of the option held, and the difference accrues to the spread.
rationales.C: A long calendar spread wants the written near-term option to expire worthless, so a large directional move before that expiration works against the position rather than for it. Profiting from an imminent large move is the objective of a long straddle or a single long option, not of a position that is short near-dated premium.

questions.stem: The outlook of a trader entering a long calendar spread is most likely:

options.A: no directional view, with the price expected to stay flat permanently.
options.B: a directional view, with the price move not expected to be imminent.
options.C: a directional view, with a large price move expected imminently.

rationales.A: The calendar spread trader does hold a directional opinion on the stock; what is absent is any expectation that the move is imminent. A view that the price will stay flat permanently would argue for writing options at both expirations, whereas the longer-dated option is bought and held precisely in order to express the eventual directional view.
rationales.B: The calendar spread trader has a directional opinion on the stock but does not believe that the price movement is imminent. Rather, the trader sees an opportunity to capture time value in one or more shorter-lived options that are expected to expire worthless. The position therefore combines a longer-term bullish or bearish outlook, expressed through the longer-dated option that is purchased, with a near-term neutral outlook, monetized through the shorter-dated option that is written.
rationales.C: An imminent large move is the outcome that damages the written near-term leg, which the trader needs to expire worthless. A long calendar spread wants near-term price stability first, and the directional move only later, after the short-dated option has expired.

questions.stem: With respect to exposure to implied volatility, a long calendar spread is most likely:

options.A: vega-neutral.
options.B: short volatility.
options.C: long volatility.

rationales.A: The vegas of the two legs do not cancel. Vega rises with time to expiration, so the longer-term option the spread is long carries a higher vega than the shorter-term option it is short, leaving a positive net vega rather than a neutral one.
rationales.B: The net vega is positive rather than negative. The position is long the higher-vega distant option and short the lower-vega near-term option, so it gains when implied volatility rises and loses when implied volatility falls — the opposite of a short volatility strategy.
rationales.C: A long calendar spread, in which the shorter-maturity option is sold and the longer-maturity option is purchased, is a long volatility trading strategy because the longer-term option has a higher vega than the shorter-term option, leaving the position with positive net vega. The maximum profit is obtained when the short-term option expires worthless and implied volatility then surges, increasing the price of the remaining long-term option.

questions.stem: A profitable calendar spread position is most likely:

options.A: short, when implied volatility falls.
options.B: short, when implied volatility rises.
options.C: long, when implied volatility falls.

rationales.A: A big move in the underlying market or a decrease in implied volatility will help a short calendar spread, whereas a stable market or an increase in implied volatility will help a long calendar spread. The short calendar spread sells the longer-dated option and buys the nearer-dated one, so it is net short vega; because the distant option carries the larger vega, a decline in implied volatility reduces the value of the option the position is short by more than it reduces the value of the option it is long. Calendar spreads are therefore sensitive both to movement of the underlying and to changes in implied volatility.
rationales.B: Rising implied volatility helps the long calendar spread, not the short one. The long calendar spread is net long the more distant option, which has the greater vega, so an increase in implied volatility raises its value by more than it raises the value of the short near-dated leg. The short calendar spread sits on the other side of that trade and benefits instead from falling implied volatility, or from a large move in the underlying.
rationales.C: A long calendar spread benefits from rising implied volatility, not a decrease, because it is net long the higher-vega distant option. A stable market does favor the long calendar spread, since the near-dated option it has sold decays faster than the distant option it holds, but pairing that stable market with a decline in implied volatility reverses the vega effect and works against the position.

questions.stem: Implied volatility is best described as:

options.A: the volatility that equates an option's model price to its market price.
options.B: the standard deviation of the underlying's returns over the past year.
options.C: the annualized standard deviation of the underlying's recent daily returns.

rationales.A: Implied volatility is not observable as such; it is derived from an option pricing model, such as the Black-Scholes-Merton model, and it is the value that equates the model price of an option to its market price. All of the other inputs to the model, including the option's strike price, the price of the underlying, the time to expiration and the risk-free interest rate, are observable, so volatility is the single unknown that can be backed out of the traded option price. Implied volatilities therefore incorporate investors' expectations about the future course of financial asset returns and the level of market uncertainty associated with them.
rationales.B: The standard deviation of the underlying's realized returns over the past year is historical, or realized, volatility. It looks backward at returns that have already occurred, whereas implied volatility is extracted from current option prices and is forward looking, which is why the two can diverge sharply when expectations shift.
rationales.C: Annualizing the standard deviation of recent daily returns produces a realized, or historical, volatility estimate, scaled up by the square root of the number of trading periods in a year.
