Implied volatility is instead backed out of current option prices as the value that equates the model price, from the Black-Scholes-Merton model for example, to the observed market price.

questions.stem: For options on the same underlying, implied volatility across strikes most likely shows:

options.A: higher implied volatilities on out-of-the-money puts.
options.B: higher implied volatilities on out-of-the-money calls.
options.C: equal implied volatilities at every strike.

rationales.A: Implied volatilities for options on a specific asset may differ with strike price, that is moneyness, with side, put or call, and with time to expiration. In particular, out-of-the-money puts typically command higher implied volatilities than at-the-money or out-of-the-money calls. This phenomenon is attributed to investors' reassessments of the probabilities of negative, fat-tailed market events such as the 2007-2009 global financial crisis, and to the universal demand for downside puts as portfolio insurance against a sell-off.
rationales.B: This reverses the observed skew. It is the downside out-of-the-money puts, demanded as crash insurance, that carry the volatility premium. Investors generally have less interest in out-of-the-money calls, so those strikes trade at lower implied volatilities than at-the-money options in most markets.
rationales.C: A single implied volatility at every strike is the flat volatility assumption of the Black-Scholes-Merton model. Empirically implied volatility varies by strike, producing the volatility skew or smile, and it varies by time to expiration as well, which together is why the implied volatility surface is typically not flat.

questions.stem: An implied volatility curve is most likely described as a volatility smile when its shape is:

options.A: downward sloping.
options.B: U-shaped.
options.C: identical to a skew.

rationales.A: A downward-sloping line is not the smile. The smile is U-shaped: the implied volatilities priced into both out-of-the-money puts and out-of-the-money calls trade at a premium to the implied volatilities of at-the-money options, so the curve turns up at both ends rather than sloping in a single direction. A curve that is flat, meanwhile, is neither a smile nor a skew but the constant volatility the Black-Scholes-Merton model assumes.
rationales.B: When the implied volatilities priced into both out-of-the-money puts and out-of-the-money calls trade at a premium to the implied volatilities of at-the-money options, the curve is U-shaped and is called a volatility smile, because it resembles the shape of a smile. The more common shape of the implied volatility curve, however, is a volatility skew, where implied volatility increases for out-of-the-money puts and decreases for out-of-the-money calls as the strike price moves away from the current price. This shape persists across asset classes and over time because investors generally have less interest in out-of-the-money calls, whereas out-of-the-money puts have found universal demand as portfolio insurance against a market sell-off.
rationales.C: The two shapes are not the same. The smile is the symmetric U, with both tails bid up above at-the-money implied volatility. The skew is asymmetric: implied volatility is elevated for out-of-the-money puts and declines for out-of-the-money calls as the strike moves away from the current price, and it is the more commonly observed of the two shapes.

questions.stem: A sharp increase in the level of the volatility skew accompanied by a surge in implied volatility most likely indicates:

options.A: an imbalance in the supply of and demand for options.
options.B: bullish market sentiment.
options.C: an inverted term structure of implied volatility.

rationales.A: When the implied volatility is significantly higher, relative to historical levels, for puts with strike prices below the underlying asset's price, it means that there is an imbalance in the supply of and demand for options. A sharp increase in the level of the skew, accompanied by a surge in the absolute level of implied volatility, is an indicator that market sentiment is turning bearish. In contrast, higher implied volatilities relative to historical levels for calls with strike prices above the underlying asset's price indicate that investors are bullish and that demand for out-of-the-money calls to take on upside exposure is strong.
rationales.B: The signal runs bearish, not bullish. Investors bidding up downside puts, which is what lifts the level of the skew, reveals demand for crash protection. Bullish sentiment shows up the other way round, as relatively high implied volatilities on out-of-the-money calls bought to take on upside exposure.
rationales.C: A rising skew accompanied by a surge in implied volatility is a directional sentiment signal, not merely an artifact of the term structure. The skew is measured across strikes at a given expiration, and its increase reflects an imbalance in the supply of and demand for options that points to sentiment turning bearish.

questions.stem: In the 90-110 volatility skew measure, the 90% moneyness option is most likely:

options.A: a put struck at 90% of the underlying's price.
options.B: a 100% moneyness option at a longer expiration.
options.C: a call struck at 110% of the underlying's price.

rationales.A: The 90% moneyness option is a put with strike X equal to 90% of the current underlying price S; thus X/S = 90%. The 110% moneyness of the call is calculated in the same way, with X/S = 110%. The volatility skew is then calculated as the difference between the implied volatilities of the 90% put and the 110% call. A positive skew number, meaning the put implied volatility exceeds the call implied volatility, reflects the fat-tail insurance premium investors pay for downside protection.
rationales.B: Time to expiration is held constant in this measure, which differences implied volatility across strikes: the implied volatility of the 90% moneyness put less the implied volatility of the 110% moneyness call. Comparing at-the-money options at different expirations describes the term structure of implied volatility instead, the other dimension of the implied volatility surface.
rationales.C: The two legs are the other way round. The 90% moneyness leg is a put struck at X/S = 90%, below the current underlying price, and the call leg sits at 110% moneyness, above it. The skew is the put implied volatility less the call implied volatility.

questions.stem: The implied volatility surface is best described as a plot of implied volatility against:

options.A: strike price and the underlying's current price.
options.B: strike price and days to expiration.
options.C: strike price only.

rationales.A: The two horizontal dimensions of the surface are days to expiration and strike price, with implied volatility plotted on the third axis. The underlying's current price is a single observable input, used to express moneyness as the ratio of strike to spot, rather than an axis of the surface.
rationales.B: The implied volatility surface can be thought of as a three-dimensional plot, for put and call options on the same underlying asset, of days to expiration on the x-axis, option strike prices on the y-axis and implied volatilities on the z-axis. It simultaneously shows the volatility skew, or smile, across strikes and the term structure of implied volatility across maturities. Because implied volatility varies across option maturities and displays skew across strikes, the surface is typically not flat, as the Black-Scholes-Merton model may suggest.
rationales.C: Plotting implied volatility against strike price alone gives a single smile or skew curve, which is one slice of the surface taken at a fixed expiration. The surface adds the days-to-expiration dimension and is therefore three-dimensional.

drills.los_text: identify and evaluate appropriate option strategies consistent with given investment objectives

questions.stem: An investor with a bearish view on the underlying who also expects implied volatility to decrease would most appropriately:

options.A: buy puts.
options.B: buy a straddle.
options.C: write calls.

rationales.A: Buying puts does express the bearish view, but a long put is long vega and long premium. If implied volatility declines as expected, the fall in volatility works against the position and erodes the option's value alongside time decay. Buying puts is the appropriate choice for a bearish view combined with rising implied volatility, not falling implied volatility.
rationales.B: A long straddle is neutral on direction and is bought to profit from a large move in the underlying or from a rise in implied volatility. It does not express the bearish view, and because it is long vega on both legs it loses value when implied volatility declines, with time decay running against it as well.
rationales.C: A bearish outlook combined with an expected decrease in implied volatility is most appropriately expressed by writing calls. Writing a call generates premium income and profits as long as the market does not rise, and because the writer is short vega, the expected decline in volatility works in the writer's favor as well. Time decay also accrues to the writer, so if volatilities are expected to fall, writing a call would likely be a profitable strategy.

questions.stem: An investor with a bullish view on the underlying who also expects implied volatility to decrease would most appropriately:

options.A: write puts.
options.B: buy a straddle.
options.C: buy calls.

rationales.A: When implied volatilities are expected to fall, writing a put represents an alternative strategy for taking advantage of a bullish market view with declining volatility. If the view is realized, the position will likely be profitable, because as the stock rises and implied volatility decreases, the short put moves farther out of the money and its price will decrease, so the writer keeps the premium collected. The short put is short vega, so the expected volatility decline adds to the gain, as does time decay.
rationales.B: A long straddle is a direction-neutral purchase of volatility, held to profit from a large move either way or from a rise in implied volatility. It does not express the bullish view, and as a long-vega, long-premium position it loses value when implied volatility falls.
rationales.C: Buying calls expresses the bullish view but is long vega and long premium, so it is the preferred choice when implied volatility is expected to rise. With volatility expected to fall, the decline in implied volatility works against the long call alongside time decay, which is why writing puts is the better fit for this combination of views.

questions.stem: An investor who is neutral on the direction of the underlying but expects implied volatility to increase would most appropriately:

options.A: write a straddle.
options.B: buy a bull call spread.
options.C: buy a straddle.

rationales.A: A short straddle is short volatility and short gamma; it profits when the underlying stays within a range and implied volatility falls. Selling a straddle into an expected surge in volatility puts the position on the wrong side of the vega exposure and leaves it exposed to large losses if the underlying makes a big move.
rationales.B: A bull call spread is a directional, bullish bet with limited upside and limited vega exposure. It does not suit a view that is neutral on direction, and it is not the way to monetize an expected rise in implied volatility.
rationales.C: If the investor is neutral on market direction, the appropriate strategy is a long straddle, because this strategy takes advantage of an increase in the long call and long put option prices in response to realization of the expected surge in volatility, vega and gamma. The position is profitable if the underlying rises above the upper breakeven, the strike plus the combined premiums paid, or falls below the lower breakeven, the strike less the combined premiums paid.

questions.stem: An investor expects an underlying stock to remain in a trading range, with implied volatility unchanged over the same period. The most appropriate option strategy is most likely:

options.A: A calendar spread.
options.B: A long straddle.
options.C: A short straddle.

rationales.A: A calendar spread combines a longer-term directional outlook with a near-term neutral outlook. It is typically implemented in option markets characterized by low implied volatility when the underlying stock is expected to remain in a trading range, but only until the maturity of the short-term option. The position's delta is approximately zero while its gamma is not zero, which matches a view that is neutral on direction and expects implied volatility to hold steady rather than move in either direction.
rationales.B: Buying a straddle is neutral on direction, but it is the trading-range strategy for an investor who expects implied volatility to increase. Both the call and the put are purchased, so premium is paid on both legs and the position needs a rise in implied volatility, or a move out of the range, to recover that outlay. With volatility expected to be unchanged, the long straddle pays for something the investor does not expect to receive.
rationales.C: Writing a straddle is also neutral on direction, but it is the trading-range strategy for an investor who expects implied volatility to decrease. Premium is collected on both the short call and the short put, and the position is designed to earn that premium as implied volatility falls. The outlook here is for volatility to remain unchanged rather than to decline, so the short straddle does not match the stated view.

questions.stem: A long risk reversal is best described as:

options.A: Long puts and short calls, a bearish position.
options.B: Long calls and short puts, a bullish position.
options.C: A delta-neutral position with no directional exposure.

rationales.A: Long puts combined with short calls is the short risk reversal, the bearish mirror image of the structure described here. Pairing the bearish leg combination with the long risk reversal reverses the position: the long risk reversal is the bullish side of the pair.
rationales.B: The combined position in which the investor is long calls and short puts is a long risk reversal, and it is used to implement a bullish view. The investor buys the calls to capture the upside and sells the puts to lower the cost of the long position in the underlying asset that will be established upon exercising the options. The combined position therefore aligns with a bullish view on the underlying together with an outlook for declining implied volatility, since both legs benefit as the premium paid away falls.
rationales.C: The structure is directional, and specifically bullish, rather than delta-neutral: the long calls and the short puts both gain as the underlying rises, so the net delta is positive. Its purpose is to lower the cost of an upside view by financing the calls with the puts, not to isolate exposure to volatility.

questions.stem: Of the following statements about buying call bull spreads and put bear spreads rather than outright options, the one that is most likely correct is:

options.A: Outright option purchases always cost less than spreads.
options.B: Spreads suit a directional view in a market that is not clearly trending.
options.C: Spreads suit conviction in an extreme move beyond the short strike.

rationales.A: The spread is the cheaper structure, not the more expensive one. A spread is normally constructed by buying one option and writing another, and the premium received on the short leg offsets the cost of the long leg, which reduces the total outlay for a modest directional view.
rationales.B: The purchase of call or put spreads tends to be most appropriate when the investor has a bullish view, in the case of a call bull spread, or a bearish view, in the case of a put bear spread, but the underlying market is not clearly trending upward or downward. Such spreads are also a way to reduce the total cost of the position, given that the spread is normally constructed by buying one option and writing another, so the premium collected on the written option offsets part of the premium paid on the purchased option.
rationales.C: Conviction in an extreme move argues for outright options rather than spreads. The short leg of a spread caps the payoff beyond its strike, so an investor who expects the underlying to travel well past that strike gives up the part of the move they are most confident about.

questions.stem: The implied volatility of out-of-the-money puts on a stock is relatively higher than the implied volatility of nearer-to-the-money puts. Relative to a flat implied volatility curve, the cost of a put bear spread on that stock is most likely:

options.A: Unaffected.
options.B: Higher.
options.C: Lower.

rationales.A: The two legs of the spread sit at different points on the implied volatility curve, so the shape of that curve prices directly into the net premium. A skew that lifts the implied volatility of out-of-the-money puts relative to nearer-to-the-money puts cannot leave the net cost of a position that is short one and long the other unchanged.
rationales.B: This has the legs the wrong way round. In the put bear spread, the lower-strike, deeper out-of-the-money put, which is the leg carrying the relatively higher implied volatility, is sold, so the richer premium is received, while the purchased nearer-to-the-money put is relatively less expensive. The skew therefore works in the investor's favor and makes the spread cheaper rather than more expensive.
rationales.C: If the implied volatility curve is skewed, with the implied volatility of out-of-the-money puts relatively higher than for nearer-to-the-money options, the cost of a bearish spread is even lower. This is because in the put bear spread the lower exercise price, more out-of-the-money and therefore relatively more expensive put is sold, and the higher exercise price, nearer-to-the-money and relatively less expensive put is purchased. The investor collects the richer skewed premium and pays the cheaper one, so the net debit shrinks.

drills.los_text: demonstrate the use of options to achieve targeted equity risk exposures

questions.stem: Parker holds 5,000 shares of MNZA at $169 per share and needs to raise about $30,000 within six months. His adviser's firm is bearish on MNZA over that horizon, and Parker is willing to part with the shares. The most appropriate recommendation is:

options.A: Write slightly out-of-the-money calls.
options.B: Buy protective puts.
options.C: Write deep in-the-money calls.

rationales.A: Writing 50 of the slightly out-of-the-money MAY 170 calls at a premium of $6.45 generates $6.45 × 100 × 50 = $32,250, which covers the $30,000 need with a small margin. Because the firm is bearish on MNZA over the six-month horizon and Parker is willing to sell the shares, the risk of having the shares called away at 170, above today's $169, is acceptable. The nearby alternatives fail on one leg or the other: the MAY 165 call would generate more than enough income at $9.10 × 100 × 50 = $45,500, but it is in the money with a high likelihood of the shares being called away at expiration; the MAY 175 call would generate only $4.03 × 100 × 50 = $20,150, about two-thirds of the projected need; and the MAY 180 call would generate only $2.50 × 100 × 50 = $12,500.
rationales.B: Protective puts cost premium rather than raise it, so buying them moves Parker further from the $30,000 he needs instead of closer to it. Writing covered calls is what converts the existing shareholding into cash, and it remains consistent with the firm's bearish six-month outlook, under which the upside given up is unlikely to be missed.
rationales.C: A deep in-the-money strike maximizes the premium collected but courts near-certain assignment at an exercise price below the current $169, so Parker would deliver the shares for less than they are worth today, and assignment risk is high rather than absent. The slightly out-of-the-money strike balances the cash raised, $32,250, against assignment terms Parker can accept.

questions.stem: Quintera wants to buy 50,000 shares of MNZA, currently trading at $169, but only at $165 or below, and writes 500 MAY 165 puts at a premium of $5.30. If MNZA trades below the strike at expiration, the effective purchase price per share is closest to:

rationales.A: The firm keeps the premium of 500 × 100 × $5.30 = $265,000 regardless of what the shares do. If the puts are exercised, the firm pays 50,000 × $165 = $8,250,000 for the shares, so the net cost of the purchase is $8,250,000 - $265,000 = $7,985,000, which on 50,000 shares is an effective purchase price of $7,985,000/50,000 = $159.70 per share. For any price below the strike the effective purchase price is always X - p = $165 - $5.30 = $159.70, which is the breakeven point of the short put position.
rationales.B: This is the exercise price, the gross amount paid per share on assignment, and it ignores the $265,000 of premium the firm keeps whatever happens. The premium is income that reduces the net outlay, so the effective price is the strike less the premium received, X - p, not the strike itself.
rationales.C: This is the market price of MNZA before the puts were written, and it is the price Quintera was unwilling to pay. Writing the puts obligates the firm to buy at the $165 strike if the shares fall below it, and the $5.30 premium received lowers the effective cost further still.

questions.stem: With the VIX at 14.87 and front-month VIX futures at 15.60, Wu buys a 15.60-strike VIX call at a premium of 2.00 and sells an equal number of 14.75-strike VIX puts at a premium of 1.55. The net cost per contract and the breakeven level of the VIX futures at expiry are closest to:

options.A: Net cost 3.55, breakeven 14.30.
options.B: Net cost 3.55, breakeven 19.15.
options.C: Net cost 0.45, breakeven 16.05.

rationales.A: This sums the two premiums instead of netting them. The 14.75 put is sold, so its 1.55 premium is received and partially finances the call, giving a net cost of 2.00 - 1.55 = 0.45 per contract rather than 3.55. The 14.30 breakeven then subtracts the net cost from the put strike, 14.75 - 0.45, when the breakeven is set by the long call leg: call strike 15.60 plus the net cost 0.45, or 16.05. The 14.75 level matters as the point below which the short puts begin to lose, not as the breakeven.
rationales.B: The 3.55 figure adds the two premiums, 2.00 + 1.55, as though both options were purchased. The 14.75 put is written, so the 1.55 premium offsets the cost of the call and the net cost is 2.00 - 1.55 = 0.45 per contract. The 19.15 breakeven compounds that error by adding the overstated cost to the call strike, 15.60 + 3.55; with the correct net cost the breakeven is 15.60 + 0.45 = 16.05.
rationales.C: The total cost of the strategy is 0.45 per contract, calculated as the 2.00 premium paid for the 15.60 call less the 1.55 premium received for the 14.75 put, which partially finances the purchase. At expiry the strategy is profitable if volatility spikes as anticipated and the VIX futures settle above 16.05, which is the call strike of 15.60 plus the net cost of the options, 15.60 + 0.45. Above that level the strategy gains proportionally, and below the 14.75 put strike it loses proportionally to its exposure through the short puts.

questions.stem: A client is bullish on Markle, now trading at £60 and expected to reach £70 within three months, with implied volatility expected to be unchanged. Three three-month calls are available: the £58 strike at £4.00 (delta 0.6295), the £60 strike at £3.00 (delta 0.5227), and the £70 strike at £0.40 (delta 0.1184). The most appropriate long call position is:

options.A: The £70 strike call.
options.B: The £58 strike call.
options.C: The £60 strike call.

rationales.A: The £70 strike call carries by far the cheapest premium, £0.40, but its breakeven is £70.40 (£70 + £0.40), which is above the client's £70 target price. The position cannot be profitable even if the view is exactly right, so the lowest premium is not the cheapest way to express the view and this call cannot be used to implement the strategy.
rationales.B: The £58 strike call does have the highest delta of the three, 0.6295, and the lowest breakeven, £62 (£58 + £4.00). But delta measures sensitivity to a small move in the underlying, not profit earned per unit of premium committed. If the stock reaches the £70 target, this call returns (£70 - £62)/£4.00 = 2.0 per unit of premium, less than the 2.3 offered by the £60 strike, because the extra £1.00 of premium buys intrinsic value the client would have captured anyway.
rationales.C: The breakeven price of the £60 strike call is £63 (£60 + £3.00), so at expiry the position is profitable at any stock price above £63, comfortably below the £70 target. The £58 strike call breaks even lower, at £62, but delivers less profit per unit of premium, and the £70 strike call breaks even at £70.40, above the target, which rules it out. Measured per unit of premium paid if the stock reaches £70, the £58 strike returns (£70 - £62)/£4.00 = 2.0 while the £60 strike returns (£70 - £63)/£3.00 = 2.3, the best of the three. With implied volatility expected to be unchanged, there is no volatility gain to justify paying the larger premium.

questions.stem: McLaire holds 100,000 shares of Relais Corp at €42.00 and expects an earnings miss that would take the shares down by at most 10%, to €37.80. Three puts are available: the €40.00 strike at €1.45, the €42.50 strike at €1.72, and the €45.00 strike at €3.46. To keep the cost of adequate protection to a minimum, the most appropriate purchase is:

options.A: The €45.00 strike put.
options.B: The €42.50 strike put.
options.C: The €40.00 strike put.

rationales.A: The €45.00 strike put gives the most protection, but at €3.46 it is also by far the costliest, and the objective is adequate protection at minimum cost. Its breakeven is €41.54 (€45.00 - €3.46), and if the shares fall to €37.80 it returns only (€41.54 - €37.80)/€3.46 = 1.08 per unit of premium paid, against 1.73 for the €42.50 strike. It also carries less gamma, 0.0346 against 0.0460, so it gains less as the stock drops.
rationales.B: The put with a strike price of €42.50 best fits the objective of keeping the cost of adequate protection to a minimum. The three breakevens are €38.55 (€40.00 - €1.45), €40.78 (€42.50 - €1.72) and €41.54 (€45.00 - €3.46). The €40.00 strike put offers limited protection because it is profitable only below €38.55 and yields a profit of just €0.75 if the stock falls to €37.80. The €42.50 strike put offers a larger profit per unit of premium paid than the €45.00 strike put at that price: (€40.78 - €37.80)/€1.72 = 1.73 against (€41.54 - €37.80)/€3.46 = 1.08. The €42.50 strike put also has more gamma than the €45.00 strike put, 0.0460 against 0.0346, so it benefits more from a fall in the share price.
rationales.C: The €40.00 strike put is the cheapest at €1.45, but cheapness is not the test; the protection must also be adequate. It becomes profitable only below €38.55 and returns just €0.75 if the shares fall to the expected €37.80, so the hedge barely engages over the drawdown it is meant to cover.

questions.stem: Regarding an investor's choice between options and futures or forwards when establishing equity exposure, the statement that is most likely correct is:

options.A: Relative commissions alone drive the choice.
options.B: Outlook, horizon, and implied volatility expectations drive the choice.
options.C: Expected rising implied volatility makes futures the better choice.

rationales.A: Commissions are a secondary consideration in this decision. The choice of derivative that will satisfy the investment goal depends on the outlook for the underlying asset, the investment horizon, and expectations for implied volatility over that horizon, all of which can move the economics of the position far more than the difference in transaction fees.
rationales.B: The choice of derivative that will satisfy the investment goal depends on the outlook for the underlying asset, the investment horizon, and expectations for implied volatility over that horizon. Options have asymmetric payoffs and are paid for with premium, while futures have symmetric payoffs and require margin but no premium. So the relative advantage of one over the other depends on the difference in leverage available, the difference in payoff profiles, asymmetrical for options and symmetrical for futures, the shape of the volatility futures term structure, and the cost of the options compared with the cost of the index futures.
rationales.C: An expected increase in implied volatility favors options, not futures. Long option positions have positive vega and gain as implied volatility rises, whereas futures have no vega and cannot capture that gain, so zero vega is a drawback rather than an advantage under this outlook. It is an expectation of falling implied volatility that argues against paying option premium and in favor of futures.
